chapter_theme: Holding kin close as a political and material matter: kin stay when wealth goes, their love multiplies gain, and wealth's use lies in being surrounded by them. They have to be kept through giving, soft speech and absence of anger, and they can be won back once estranged.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the distinction of kin (521), kinship as cause, protection and fruit of wealth (522-524), the means of holding them (525-528), and receiving those who left and returned (529-530).

521.reading: Even when all is gone, to keep honouring old ties is found only among kin.
521.nuance: பழைமை points back to shared history. Parimelazhagar takes it as help the fallen man gave when he had means, which turns kin loyalty into a kind of remembered debt. Kalaignar turns the description into a definition: those with this trait are kin.

522.reading: If kin whose love doesn't lapse come together, they yield many gains that keep on branching.
522.nuance: Pope's flower and fadeless blossom come from reading அருப்பு as a bud. The commentators read it as branching, கிளைத்தல், which gives a neat play: கிளை also means kin. So kin make wealth put out kin of its own, though that last step is my reading.

523.reading: The life of one who doesn't mingle freely is like a broad tank filling with water, with no bank.
523.nuance: The tank does fill: the failure isn't in earning. Without kin, the wealth has nothing to hold it and spreads away uselessly. அளவளாவு is intimacy, and Parimelazhagar explains it through mutual sharing of mind, so mere proximity isn't enough.

524.reading: The fruit of having gained wealth is to live surrounded by one's kin.
524.nuance: It is striking how far this goes: a whole purpose for wealth in four words. Parimelazhagar's reason keeps it in Porul: it is what enables ruling free of enemies. Read without him, it is more tender than that.

525.reading: One who can give and speak pleasantly will be surrounded by kin in layer upon layer.
525.nuance: Parimelazhagar identifies these with the Sanskrit policies of dāna and sāma. So the tender acts of the household are also two of the four instruments of statecraft, which he used in 467 against enemies.

526.reading: No one on earth has more of a following than one who gives greatly and doesn't cherish anger.
526.nuance: பேணான் doesn't mean he has no anger, only that he doesn't tend it. Parimelazhagar even takes it as not exceeding what a king needs. In 487 anger is nursed within against enemies. The verses may simply be about different audiences.

527.reading: Crows don't hide, they call and eat; gain too belongs only to those of that nature.
527.nuance: A humble bird is the model for royal conduct. The verse's உம் says gain too comes this way, and Parimelazhagar concludes that sharing yields wealth as well as virtue and pleasure. Hiding, கரவா, is what is excluded, so a person's private hoard is the fault.

528.reading: If a king looks at people not in common but by rank, many will live looking to that.
528.nuance: A real problem: equal treatment drives away those who see themselves as higher. Parimelazhagar openly gives that as the reason.

positions.position: Each kinsman is to be regarded according to his own standing; treating all alike would make the eminent leave.
positions.quote: எல்லாரையும் ஒரு தன்மையராக நோக்காது அரசன் தத்தம் தகுதிக்கு ஏற்ப நோக்குமாயின்

positions.position: The verse is about singling out one person: it is the advice to appoint a crown prince.
All people are equal, and regard should follow ability, not rank.

529.reading: Those who were kin and left will return to kinship when the cause of discord is gone.

positions.position: The cause was in the king. If he removes it, they come back by themselves, as natural affection returns without being won again.
positions.quote: அவ்வமராமைக் காரணம் தன் மாட்டு இல்லையாகத் தானே உளதாம்.

positions.position: The cause was their pretext. They come back on realising it doesn't hold up.

530.reading: One who left and came back for a reason, the king should accept with care after attending to it.
530.nuance: The contrast with 529 is subtle, as Parimelazhagar notes: there a reason for leaving is removed, and here there was none for leaving, only one for returning. He advises to grant what the person came for, but stay cautious: otherwise he may go to the enemy, but he has also shown no love.

links.note: Both show wealth as a full tank. In 215 it is a public pond serving all, and in 523 it has no banks. The first image is about access, the second about containment: wealth has to be held to be shared.
212 says all wealth earned exists to serve the worthy. 524 says its fruit is being surrounded by kin. Both state the purpose of wealth, with different beneficiaries, and neither mentions the other.
521 declares that kin stay in adversity. 796 calls adversity a measuring rod for kin, which assumes some won't stay. A generalisation about kin in 53 becomes a test of them in 80.
